_comment: Shahnama of Firdausi, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vols. III-IV: Kamus of Kashan, Rustam vs the Khan of Chin, Puladwand, and the Great War of Kai Khusrau. Paraphrase passages with notes.

title.en: Rustam on Foot Slays Ashkabus of Kashan
title.zh: 徒步的魯斯塔姆誅卡什安的阿什卡布斯

region.zh: 哈馬萬山前平原（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. III, Kamus sec. 28

summary.en: Ashkabus of Kashan rides out challenging the Iranians and smashes Ruhham's helm, till matchless Rustam comes on foot with bow slung and arrows in his belt: my mother called me by this name — 'Thy death!'; do lions, crocodiles, and leopards fight on horseback in thy country? Ashkabus laughs in astonishment, and Rustam shoots an arrow at the breast of his fine steed: sit by thy noble comrade and nurse its head! Then, taking his bow of Chach, he set his thumbstall to the deer-hide string; the bent bow sang; the shaft's point bussed his finger; he loosed and struck the breast of Ashkabus — the sky kissed Rustam's hand — and he of Kashan expired. The Khan's heart aged when he beheld the feathers and the point: their arrows are like spears!
summary.zh: 卡什安勇將阿什卡布斯叫陣、擊碎魯哈姆的頭盔；魯斯塔姆竟徒步出戰，肩掛弓、腰插箭：「我母親給我取名——『你的死期』！你們那裡的獅子、鱷魚也騎馬打仗嗎？」一箭射翻其戰馬，再取喬赫硬弓搭箭——弓弦輕吟、箭吻指腹——一箭貫胸！天地喝彩；卡尚人當場斃命。可汗見那箭羽箭鏃，頓時心冷：「他們的箭竟如長矛！」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: The peerless Rustam answered: hapless one! why askest thou my name among the folk? My mother called me by this name — Thy death! Fate made me for the hammer of thy helm. He of Kashan replied: without a horse thou givest up thyself to slaughtering! Then peerless Rustam: senseless challenger! Hast thou ne'er seen foot-soldiers lay proud heads beneath the stones? Do lions, crocodiles, and leopards fight on horseback in thy country?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kamus sec. 28 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He marked the pride of Ashkabus in his fine steed, and shot an arrow at its breast; the charger fell headforemost. Rustam laughed and cried aloud: sit by thy noble comrade! Prithee nurse its head and rest thee from the fight awhile. Then Ashkabus, his body quivering, strung up his bow and showered shafts on Rustam, who exclaimed: in vain thou weariest thy wicked soul, thine arms, and body.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kamus sec. 28 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Choosing from his girdle a shaft of poplar wood he drew it forth bright-pointed, feathered with four eagle-plumes; then took his bow of Chach in hand and set his thumbstall to the deer-hide string; he straightened his left arm, curved his right; the bent bow sang; the shaft's point reached his ear; the deer-hide hummed; the shaft's point bussed his finger and its notch was at his back; he loosed and struck the breast of Ashkabus; the sky kissed Rustam's hand. He of Kashan expired, thou wouldst have said: his mother never bare him!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kamus sec. 28 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Kamus of Kashan Taken by the Sixty Coils

region.zh: 哈馬萬戰場（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. III, Kamus sec. 32

summary.en: The peerless Rustam let loose the twisted lasso from its straps and took his massive mace; Kamus said: bluster not so much about a thread of sixty coils. The lion roareth bravely on catching sight of game, said Rustam; now shalt thou see how tight the knots will hold. Kamus let out with his glittering glaive to sever Rustam's head; the point alighted on Rakhsh's neck and clave the battle-mail, but failed to wound. The elephantine hero coiled, whirled, and flung the lasso round his foe, then spurred away and made the leather fast beneath his thigh while Rakhsh flew eagle-like. Kamus sought by force to break the twisted thong, becoming frantic, but the raw hide held: now this illustrious warrior's helm and hauberk are his shroud, his crown is dust, and his juppon the grave.
summary.zh: 卡穆斯譏其「六十圈的線繩」；魯斯塔姆答：「獅見獵物而吼——你就知道這結有多緊！」卡穆斯的利劍劈在拉赫什頸甲上未能傷人；英雄套索飛出、纏住敵腰，一抖韁繩、驅駿馬如鷹疾馳——任憑卡穆斯如何發狂掙扎，生牛皮紋絲不斷。英雄拖其至眾將之前：「他的頭盔鎧甲成了壽衣，王冠化塵，戰袍即是墳墓！」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: The peerless Rustam let loose the twisted lasso from its straps, and took his massive mace as for a strife of chiefs; he roared like some mad elephant as he advanced with lasso on his arm and mace in hand. Kamus said: bluster not so much about a thread of sixty coils. The lion roareth bravely, Rustam said, on catching sight of game; now shalt thou see how tight the knots will hold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kamus sec. 32 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kamus the valiant urged his dun steed on, and let out with his glittering glaive, intent to sever Rustam's head; the point alighted on Rakhsh's neck and clave the battle-mail, but failed to wound. The elephantine hero coiled, whirled, and flung the lasso round his foe, then spurred away and made the leather fast beneath his thigh while Rakhsh flew eagle-like. Kamus sought by force to break the twisted thong, becoming frantic, but the raw hide held.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kamus sec. 32 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The elephantine hero, checking Rakhsh, wheeled, jerked Kamus headforemost to the ground, came up, secured him in the lasso's coils, and said to him: thou art not dangerous now. In vain are all thy charms and spells; thy soul hath made a fruitless bargain with the Div. On what wise do ye purpose slaying him? Then Rustam flung Kamus upon the ground before the chiefs; the warriors left their ranks, hacked his body with their scimitars, and drenched the stones and dust beneath with blood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Kamus sec. 32 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Kafur the Man-eater and the City of Bidad
title.zh: 食人者卡富爾與「不義之城」

region.en: City of Bidad in Sughd (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 粟特比達德城（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. III, Khan of Chin sec. 20

summary.en: On marching one stage thence Rustam saw a city by name Bidad, a hold inhabited by folk whose only food was human flesh: the flesh of growing youths alone was served at the loathly king's board. The king's name was Kafur; when he heard that a host led by a famed chief approached, he armed as did his pard-like people, skilled lasso-flingers and stones and anvils in the fray. Gustaham bids Bizhan tell Rustam to come with ten score cavaliers; Kafur flung his lasso o'er the son of Zal, who ducked his head; then Rustam raised his war-cry like an angry elephant, smote his head-piece with the mace, which smashed together helmet, head, and neck: his brains ran down his nostrils, and Kafur the warrior fell.
summary.zh: 行軍途中魯斯塔姆望見「不義之城」比達德——城中人以人肉為食，少年之肉供奉暴君餐桌！食人王卡富爾率豹一般彪悍的套索手迎戰；古斯塔哈姆遣比讚求援。卡富爾擲出套索，魯斯塔姆低頭躲過，隨即如怒象般吶喊、掄錘猛擊——盔、顱、頸一齊粉碎，腦漿自鼻孔流出，食人者當場斃命！

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; man-eater episode. No living community restriction.

passages.text: On marching one stage thence he saw a city by name Bidad, a hold inhabited by folk whose only food was human flesh. The lovely there were ever perishing, while at the table of a king so loathly the flesh of growing youths alone was served. Those slaves that were the goodliest supplied the provand for the monarch's board; such was his food. The king's name was Kafur; he held the city by patent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Khan of Chin sec. 20 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: When he heard that from Iran a host, led by a famed and warlike chief, approached, he armed as did his pard-like people, who were skilled lasso-flingers, cavaliers, and stones and anvils in the fray. Gustaham said to Bizhan in haste: ride hence; tell Rustam: pause not, but come with ten score cavaliers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Khan of Chin sec. 20 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kafur came rushing with a furious charge against the royal and fruit-bearing Tree, and hurled his sword, as though it were an arrow, but Rustam received it on his shield and took no harm. Kafur next flung his lasso o'er the son of Zal, who ducked his head; then Rustam raised his war-cry like an angry elephant, whereat Kafur stood still in blank amaze, and Rustam smote his head-piece with the mace, which smashed together helmet, head, and neck: his brains ran down his nostrils, and Kafur the warrior fell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Khan of Chin sec. 20 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Rustam Uproots Puladwand Like a Plane-tree
title.zh: 魯斯塔姆如拔山楊般揪起普拉達萬德

region.en: Plain of Machin and Chin (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 馬秦與秦地平原（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. III, Khan of Chin secs. 24-25

summary.en: Afrasiyab summons the warrior-div Puladwand to his aid, and Tus, Giv, Ruhham, and Bizhan are all unhorsed. Rustam challenges the ill-conditioned div, and elephantine Rustam with his mace strikes his foe's head: all present heard the crash. When the mace fails, Puladwand says: wrestling is the test 'twixt man and man; take we each other by the leathern belt. Afrasiyab, breaking troth, urges him on: if thou gett'st him down in wrestling rip him open with thy dagger. Then, like a lion, reaching out he clutched the chest and neck of that fierce Crocodile, and, straining hard, uprooted Puladwand, as though he were a plane-tree, from his place, raised him aloft, dashed him upon the ground, and uttered praises to Almighty God.
summary.zh: 阿弗拉西亞卜召來魔王戰將普拉達萬德，圖斯、吉夫、魯哈姆、比讚接連墜馬。魯斯塔姆出陣，一錘擊其頭顱——全場聽得巨響！魔王懼其虎皮鎧甲，提議角力定勝負；暴君卻背信喝令「摔倒便以匕首剖之」。然而獅爪般的英雄抓住那兇鱷的胸頸，奮力一拔——如拔山楊樹般將魔王連根揪起、高舉過頂、狠狠摜地，並讚頌全能之神！

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; pairs with the Sohrab and Human wrestling duels. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Then closing with the div he threw his lasso, but Puladwand, brave horseman though he was, ducked in alarm, he had had fight enough. Consider now the fire of mine attack, my lasso, courage, might, and enterprise, said the div; thou shalt behold no traces of thy Shah, his nobles, or his mighty men henceforth, for I will give thine army to Afrasiyab.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Khan of Chin sec. 24 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then both the warriors wheeled till Puladwand, whose massive mace fell but without effect on Rustam's tiger-skin and coat of steel, said: wrestling is the test 'twixt man and man; take we each other by the leathern belt, that we may know which one the will of fate dismisseth worsted from the battlefield.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Khan of Chin sec. 24 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Giv marked the king's wild words: observe Afrasiyab, his eagerness, and wild words! He hath come forth to inflame the heart of thine antagonist and prompt him to use his dagger in a wrestling-bout. Then, like a lion, reaching out Rustam clutched the chest and neck of that fierce Crocodile, and, straining hard, uprooted Puladwand, as though he were a plane-tree, from his place, raised him aloft, dashed him upon the ground, and uttered praises to Almighty God.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Khan of Chin secs. 24-25 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

region.zh: 烏滸水渡口（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. IV, Great War sec. 14

summary.en: As soon as Kai Khusrau had passed the river he banished banqueting, repose, and sleep, and sent this proclamation forth: let no man be in terror at our coming, but offer prayer for us to holy God. He gave great largess to the mendicants, thence departed to the march of Sughd, and saw a novel world, the home of owls, lavishing treasure in eagerness for its prosperity. He harangued his host: as for the Turkmans who submit themselves, and in their hearts repent of making war, fight not against them, and shed not their blood — but if any whose vengeful heart remaineth recusant shall strive against you, then bloodshed and harrying are permitted you. He traversed in this way a hundred leagues, depopulating stronghold, hill, and plain.
summary.zh: 大軍一渡烏滸水，霍斯勞即戒宴樂、戒酣眠，並傳諭：「我軍所至，爾等勿懼；請向聖神為我們祈禱。」他厚賜貧者，兵發粟特——那「貓頭鷹的國度」；並告誡全軍：「凡棄戰歸順、真心悔過的突厥人，不得加害；唯有負隅頑抗者，方可誅討。」於是大軍橫掃百驛之地，堡壘丘陵悉數平毀。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the avenger-king's conquest of Turan. No living community restriction.

passages.text: As soon as Kai Khusrau had passed the river he banished banqueting, repose, and sleep, and, when he had transported all his troops across, he sent this proclamation forth: let no man be in terror at our coming, but offer prayer for us to holy God. He gave great largess to the mendicants, especially to those who welcomed him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Great War sec. 14 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He thence departed to the march of Sughd, and saw a novel world, the home of owls; upon that country too he lavished treasure in eagerness for its prosperity, and, whereso'er he halted, cavaliers came seeking quarter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Great War sec. 14 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Anon the Shah harangued his host and said: in that our task is different to-day, as for the Turkmans who submit themselves, and in their hearts repent of making war, fight not against them, and shed not their blood. Lead none the way to evil, but if any, whose vengeful heart remaineth recusant, shall seek to strive against you with a host, then bloodshed, harrying, and combating in any quarter are permitted you. He traversed in this way a hundred leagues, depopulating stronghold, hill, and plain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Great War sec. 14 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Afrasiyab Shuts Himself in Gang-bihisht, His Earthly Paradise
title.zh: 阿弗拉西亞卜退守「地上天堂」剛比希什特

region.zh: 秦地之外的剛比希什特（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. IV, Great War secs. 16-18

summary.en: Gang is eight leagues in length and four in breadth; men, women, children, and troops are there; no eagles soar above its battlements, none dreameth of such heights! There are provisions, palace, treasure, crown, and majesty; the country round about is called Bihisht — i.e. Paradise — where all is pleasure, peace, and happiness. Relying on his fortune Afrasiyab entered Gang-bihisht exultingly with all his arms and implements of war; he bade magicians bring up mighty stones upon the walls, stationed troops upon the ramparts, and kept a troop of smiths at work to fashion claws of steel on every side and bind them to long spears to grapple any that adventured nigh.
summary.zh: 阿弗拉西亞卜退入他自建的「地上天堂」——剛比希什特：八里縱橫、泉池棋布、寶庫王宮俱全，「鷹隼不越其雉堞，凡人難夢其高峻」！他命術士以法力運巨石築牆，塔樓遍佈甲士，又令鐵匠打造長桿鋼鉤——凡近城者，非被鉤住即被嚇退。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the fortified paradise of the Turanian king. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Gang is eight leagues in length and four in breadth; men, women, children, and troops are there; thou wilt have wealth, the foe will still toil on. No eagles soar above its battlements, none dreameth of such heights! There are provisions, palace, treasure, crown, and majesty, command, and throne and host. The country round about is called Bihisht, where all is pleasure, peace, and happiness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Great War sec. 16 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Whenas Afrasiyab had heard these words they pleased him and, relying on his fortune, he entered Gang-bihisht exultingly with all his arms and implements of war. He went about the city and beheld not e'en a hand-breadth of waste ground therein; there was a palace lifted to the sky, built by himself, a king whose word was law.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Great War sec. 16 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Afrasiyab for his own part at Gang abandoned quiet, banqueting, and sleep, arranged his catapults upon the walls, and fitted up the towers to stand a siege. He bade magicians bring up mighty stones upon the walls, and he kept a troop of smiths at work to fashion claws of steel on every side and bind them to long spears to grapple any that adventured nigh, or, if not that, to make him shun the hold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Great War sec. 17 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

region.zh: 剛比希什特王宮（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. IV, Great War sec. 22

summary.en: Afrasiyab, beholding such terror and defeat — no Jahn, no brother, no land, no throne, no realm, no gems, no treasure — farewells his throne of sovereignty: when shall I ever look on thee again upon a day of pleasure, ease, and joy? Now when he built the palace in the hold he had made a secret passage underground, and not a soldier of the army wotted that there was such a by-way underneath the castle: he made choice of ten score chiefs, and vanished by that secret souterrain, emerging he betook him to the waste, while all his kingdom wondered after him, none knowing where he was. Khusrau approached the palace, trod down his foe's star, and assumed the throne.
summary.zh: 堡破之際，阿弗拉西亞卜登樓一望——戰士死傷殆盡、兄弟俱失、江山財寶成空——他泣別御座：「幾時才能再享歡愉之日？」原來他築宮時預留了一條地下密道，全軍無一人知曉；他率兩百名酋長自密道遁入荒野，舉國驚疑、莫知所蹤。霍斯勞入城、踏碎敵星，登上那空置的王座。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; no living community restriction.

passages.text: Afrasiyab, beholding matters thus, such terror and defeat, no Jahn, no brother, no land, no throne, no realm, no gems, no treasure, cried out in very earnest, seared and sore: how wantonly heaven's vault hath dealt with us! He came down woeful from the palace-roof, farewelled his throne of sovereignty, and said: when shall I ever look on thee again upon a day of pleasure, ease, and joy?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Great War sec. 22 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now when he built the palace in the hold he made a secret passage underground, and not a soldier of the army wotted that there was such a by-way underneath the castle. He made choice of ten score chiefs, and vanished by that secret souterrain; emerging he betook him to the waste, while all his kingdom wondered after him, none knowing where he was because he vanished so suddenly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Great War sec. 22 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Khusrau approached the palace, trod down his foe's star, and assumed the throne amid the paladins with golden helms. They made abundant quest, but failed to trace that chief of nobles; then the Shah inquired of Jahn and Garsiwaz about their king: how did he go and whither hath he gone? The conquering Shah said: now that my foe hath vanished from the throne his name and purpose matter not a jot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Great War sec. 22 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Hum's Lasso: Afrasiyab and Garsiwaz Slain
title.zh: 胡姆的套索：阿弗拉西亞卜與加爾西瓦茲授首

region.zh: 流浪者之湖（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. IV, Great War sec. 44

summary.en: While these two princes were exchanging words the mind of Hum, the devotee, devised a scheme: he went upon a spit of land, and, when he saw Afrasiyab anear, undid the royal lasso from his waist and flung it, and took the monarch's head within the noose; he dragged him forth from lake to land and resigned him to the Shahs. First I allege the murder of thy brother, says Kai Khusrau; next of Naudar, that world-lord and memorial of Iraj; and thirdly that of Siyawush, whose head thou didst cut off as 'twere a sheep's. With Indian sword he smote Afrasiyab upon the neck, and flung upon the dust the swarthy form whose ears and hoary beard were red with blood; they dragged Garsiwaz shamefully in heavy bonds, and clave the chief asunder at the waist, and flung those two like mountains side by side.
summary.zh: 隱士胡姆設計擒龍：一記套索將阿弗拉西亞卜自湖畔拖上陸地，獻於王前。霍斯勞歷數其三罪：「弑叔伊拉吉、誅瑙達爾、斬西亞瓦什如屠羊！」言畢揮劍斬其頸，那黑面白鬚的軀體轟然倒地；其弟加爾西瓦茲被縛至帳前，自腰斬為兩段——如兩座山嶽並陳於野。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the end of the Turanian arch-foe. No living community restriction.

passages.text: While these two princes were exchanging words the mind of Hum, the devotee, devised a scheme; he went upon a spit of land, and, when he saw Afrasiyab anear, undid the royal lasso from his waist, and came on stalking like a savage lion, then flung the lasso that was ready coiled, and took the monarch's head within the noose. Hum dragged him forth in miserable plight, and loathing life itself, from lake to land, resigned him to the Shahs and went his way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Great War sec. 44 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: O evil-doer, answered Kai Khusrau, well worthy of reproach and infamy! First I allege the murder of thy brother, who never sought to injure noble men; next of Naudar, that famous sovereign, that world-lord and memorial of Iraj, whose neck thou clav'st with thy sharp scimitar; and thirdly that of Siyawush, like whom none seeth any horseman to recall him, whose head thou didst cut off as 'twere a sheep's. How was it possible to slay my sire and not expect an evil day like this?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Great War sec. 44 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: With Indian sword he smote Afrasiyab upon the neck, then flung upon the dust the swarthy form, whose ears and hoary beard were red with blood, while Garsiwaz his brother lost all hope; Afrasiyab's imperial throne was void; the day of his good fortune reached its close. They dragged him from the jailors shamefully in heavy bonds, on that his evil day; when in sad plight he came before Khusrau the Shah called an executioner who came with trenchant sword unsheathed, and clave the chief asunder at the waist, and they flung those two like mountains side by side.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Great War sec. 44 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.
